issues.legal_issue: A son cannot restrain execution of a mortgage decree against joint-family property for a debt personally owed by his father if the debt was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
material_facts: A father who managed a joint family mortgaged its property and personally covenanted to repay the loan.
The mortgagee obtained a decree for sale of the property against the father, and a son sought to stop the sale before it took place.
The debt was admitted to be owing by the father and was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
issues.conclusion: The son had no right to obtain an interim or final stay of the sale, even though the sale had not yet occurred and his suit had been filed before the decree for sale.
issues.legal_principle: Under the second proposition in Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad, a father may, by incurring a debt not tainted by an immoral purpose, expose joint-family property to execution for payment of that debt. The principle applies to secured as well as unsecured debts and to execution of a mortgage decree before sale. The Court relied on Luhar Amritlal Nagji v. Doshi Jayantilal Jethalal and the pious-obligation doctrine, and rejected contrary observations in Jagdish Prasad v. Hoshyar Singh, Bharamappa Murdeppa v. Hanmantappa Tippanna, Ganpati v. Rameshwar, and Abdul Hameed Sait v. Provident Investment Co. Ltd.

predicates.son_challenges_mortgage_decree_execution: A son seeks to stop execution of a mortgage decree against joint-family property mortgaged by his father as manager.
predicates.father_personally_owes_debt: The father is personally liable to repay the debt secured by the mortgage.
predicates.debt_not_illegal_or_immoral: The debt was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.

issues.definition: When a son seeks to stop execution of a mortgage decree for a debt personally owed by his father, and the debt was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose, the son cannot restrain the sale before it occurs.

issues.legal_issue: A son may impeach a mortgage of joint-family property that the father-manager made without legal necessity or payment of an antecedent debt, even after a decree on the mortgage has been passed against the father.
material_facts: A father acting as manager mortgaged joint-family property, and a son claimed that the mortgage was neither for legal necessity nor for payment of an antecedent debt.
The mortgagee obtained a decree against the father on the mortgage before the son’s challenge was finally decided.
The son sought a declaration that the mortgage and decree did not bind his interest in the property.
issues.conclusion: The decree against the father did not enlarge the mortgagee’s security or make the mortgage binding on the son’s interest; the son remained entitled to challenge the mortgage on the ground that it lacked legal necessity and was not for payment of an antecedent debt.
issues.legal_principle: The first and third propositions in Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad, read together, establish that a manager generally cannot burden joint-family property except for legal necessity and that a father-manager’s mortgage must be for legal necessity or payment of an antecedent debt to bind the estate. A decree against the father does not itself create or enlarge a mortgage over the son’s interest.

predicates.son_challenges_family_mortgage_after_dec: A son challenges the effect on his interest of a mortgage of joint-family property after a decree on the mortgage has been passed against his father.
predicates.father_managed_joint_family: The father acted as manager of the joint family when he mortgaged its property.
predicates.mortgage_lacked_legal_necessity_and_ante: The mortgage was neither for legal necessity nor for payment of an antecedent debt.

issues.definition: When a son challenges a post-decree mortgage of joint-family property made by his father-manager without legal necessity or payment of an antecedent debt, the son may challenge its effect on his interest.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgage securing a father-manager’s loan binds the joint-family property, including the son’s interest, when the loan is used partly to pay antecedent debts and partly for the joint-family business and other legal necessities.
material_facts: The father-manager borrowed money and mortgaged joint-family property to secure repayment.
Part of the loan was used to discharge antecedent debts.
The remaining loan proceeds were used for the joint-family business and other legal necessities, including family maintenance and the son’s education.
The Court found that the father was carrying on the family business and rejected evidence that he had not done so.
issues.conclusion: The mortgage in its entirety bound the joint-family property, including the son’s interest.
issues.legal_principle: Under Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad, a father-manager may mortgage the joint-family estate for legal necessity or payment of an antecedent debt. The Court found the loan was used for antecedent debts and for the family business and other legal necessities, and held that the mortgage therefore bound the property in its entirety.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges whether a father-manager’s mortgage binds joint-family property, and the loan was used partly for antecedent debts and otherwise for the family business or other legal necessities, the mortgage binds the entire property.
